summary: A salon with genuine long-term regulars who name their technicians and keep coming back for years. The reviews are good and almost none of them have ever been answered.

observations.title: Regulars name their techs and stay for years
observations.detail: Judy and Jane come up by name, and several reviewers describe returning over a long period rather than trying somewhere else. Retention like that is the hardest thing for a salon to build and you already have it.
observations.evidence: Multiple reviews name specific technicians and describe multi-year loyalty.

observations.title: Almost no reviews have a reply
observations.detail: Nearly every review, including the happy ones, sits without a response from the salon. Google quietly ranks businesses higher when each review gets answered, and a thanks on a five star review is the cheapest marketing you will ever do.
observations.evidence: Owner responses are essentially absent across the reviews read.

observations.title: The deposit-to-book step is not explained up front
observations.detail: A reviewer describes a deposit being required to secure an appointment. That is a reasonable policy for a salon with no-shows, but if a customer meets it for the first time mid-booking it reads as friction rather than as protection.
observations.evidence: A review describes a deposit requirement when securing an appointment.

questions: Who replies to reviews now, and what would it take to answer all 65?
Where does a new customer first learn about the deposit policy?
How often do you lose a booking between the enquiry and the deposit?
When Judy or Jane is fully booked, what happens to that customer?
focus: Sixty-five reviews, strong ratings, and no replies is the clearest gap here. What would change if every one got a short answer this month?
